items.definition: the total amount of money a business earns from selling goods or services, before costs are taken away
exampleSentences: The company's revenue grew by twelve percent last year.
Online sales now make up half of our total revenue.
Revenue increased even though the number of buyers stayed the same.

items.definition: the money a business keeps after subtracting all its costs from what it earns
exampleSentences: The store made a small profit in its first year.
Higher costs cut into the company's profit.
Profit rose sharply after the new product launched.

items.definition: the money a business spends in order to operate
exampleSentences: Travel expenses increased due to more overseas trips.
The company cut expenses by moving to a smaller office.
Keep every receipt so you can claim your expenses.

items.definition: a plan for how much money will be earned and spent over a period of time
exampleSentences: The team went over budget this quarter.
We increased the budget for new equipment.
A tight budget meant delaying some purchases.

items.definition: a statement about what is likely to happen in the future, based on current information
exampleSentences: The finance team prepared a forecast for the next quarter.
Our sales forecast was more optimistic than the actual results.
Analysts revised their forecast after the earnings report.

items.definition: the total profit a company makes in a particular period, often reported to investors
exampleSentences: The company's earnings beat analysts' expectations.
Earnings fell slightly compared to last year.
Investors reacted well to the strong earnings report.

items.definition: the money a business loses when its costs are higher than its income
exampleSentences: The company reported a loss for the second year in a row.
A sudden drop in sales led to a big loss.
They managed to turn a loss into a small profit.

items.definition: an increase in the size, value, or amount of something over time
exampleSentences: The company has seen steady growth over the past five years.
Growth slowed down during the difficult winter months.
Investors were pleased with the strong growth in earnings.

items.definition: a gradual decrease in the amount, value, or quality of something
exampleSentences: Sales showed a slight decline in the last quarter.
The decline in revenue worried the shareholders.

items.definition: a period of three months, often used to report a company's financial results
exampleSentences: The company reports its results every quarter.
Profits were higher in the third quarter.
This quarter's earnings surprised everyone.

items.definition: a document that lists goods or services provided and states how much money is owed
exampleSentences: The supplier sent an invoice for the last delivery.
Please pay the invoice within thirty days.
We found an error on the invoice and asked for a correction.

items.definition: the money that moves into and out of a business over a period of time
exampleSentences: Late payments can seriously hurt a small company's cash flow.
The business improved its cash flow by collecting payments faster.
Poor cash flow forced the company to delay some purchases.

items.definition: something valuable that a person or company owns
exampleSentences: The factory is one of the company's most valuable assets.
They sold several assets to pay off their debt.
A skilled team can be a company's greatest asset.

items.definition: a debt or a financial obligation that a company must pay
exampleSentences: The company's liabilities increased after it took out a large loan.
Unpaid taxes are recorded as a liability.
Reducing liabilities improved the firm's financial position.

items.definition: the value of a company's assets after all its debts have been paid
exampleSentences: Shareholder equity rose after a strong year of profits.
The founders gave up some equity to attract new investors.
A drop in equity worried long-term investors.

items.definition: a part of a company's profit that is paid to shareholders
exampleSentences: The company paid a higher dividend after a record year.
Shareholders were happy to receive a dividend again.
Some fast-growing companies choose not to pay a dividend.

items.definition: a person or organization that owns part of a company through shares
exampleSentences: Shareholders voted to approve the new budget.
The board must report the results to shareholders every quarter.
A major shareholder pushed for changes to the strategy.

items.definition: an official examination of a company's financial records to check that they are correct
exampleSentences: An outside firm conducts an audit of our accounts every year.
The audit found no serious problems.
Preparing for the audit took the finance team several weeks.

items.definition: the total amount of money a business earns from sales during a period of time
exampleSentences: Annual turnover reached ten million dollars last year.
A drop in turnover forced the company to cut costs.
Turnover grew steadily despite the difficult market.

items.definition: the regular costs of running a business, such as rent and electricity
exampleSentences: Moving to a smaller office reduced the company's overhead.
High overhead made it hard to stay profitable.
They cut overhead by switching to remote work.

items.definition: the profit a company has left after paying all its costs and taxes
exampleSentences: Net income doubled thanks to lower operating costs.
The report showed a small net income despite falling sales.
Investors focus closely on net income each quarter.

items.definition: a twelve-month period that a company uses for its financial reports, which may not match the calendar year
exampleSentences: Our fiscal year begins in April, not January.
The company set new targets for the coming fiscal year.
Results for the last fiscal year were better than expected.

items.definition: a financial document that shows what a company owns and owes at a particular time
exampleSentences: The balance sheet showed more assets than liabilities.
A strong balance sheet gave investors confidence.
The accountant updated the balance sheet at the end of the quarter.

items.definition: to earn just enough money to cover your costs, without making a profit or a loss
exampleSentences: The new store expects to break even within its first year.
It took two years for the project to break even.
They finally managed to break even after cutting overhead costs.

items.definition: an amount of money that is left over after all costs have been paid
exampleSentences: The company reported a budget surplus this year.
A surplus allowed the company to invest in new equipment.
Careful spending created a small surplus by year end.

items.definition: the amount by which spending is greater than income
exampleSentences: The department had to explain the growing deficit.
A trade deficit can affect a country's currency.
They reduced the deficit by cutting unnecessary costs.

items.definition: not yet paid or finished
exampleSentences: Several invoices remained outstanding at the end of the month.
The company chased buyers for outstanding payments.
An outstanding balance of two thousand dollars was still owed.

items.definition: the profit or benefit gained from something, compared to how much it cost
exampleSentences: The new equipment gave the company a strong return on investment.
The training program showed a clear return on investment within a year.
A low return on investment made the plan less attractive.

items.definition: comparing figures from one year to the exact same period the year before
exampleSentences: Revenue grew ten percent year-on-year.
The report compares year-on-year sales figures.
Year-on-year growth slowed in the last quarter.

items.definition: to accept officially that a debt will not be paid, or that something has lost its value, and remove it from the accounts
exampleSentences: The bank had to write off several unpaid loans.
They decided to write off the old equipment as a loss.
Companies sometimes write off bad debts at the end of the fiscal year.

lessons.title: Grammar: Present perfect vs past simple for results

items.headword: Present perfect vs past simple for results
items.definition: choosing between present perfect and past simple when reporting business results
items.explanationTR:
When we report business and financial results, we choose between the present perfect and the past simple depending on whether the time is finished or still connected to now.

• Present perfect (have/has + past participle): used when there's no finished time reference, or when a period such as 'this year' or 'so far' is still going on. It connects a past event to a present result.
  - Revenue has grown by ten percent this year.
  - The company has not published its results yet.

• Past simple: used with a finished time reference, such as 'last quarter,' 'in 2023,' or 'yesterday.'
  - Revenue grew by ten percent last quarter.
  - The company published its results in March.

• Time words are the clue: 'so far,' 'this year,' 'yet,' and 'already' usually go with the present perfect; 'last year,' 'in 2022,' and 'yesterday' go with the past simple.

• In a quarterly report, both forms often appear together: 'Earnings have improved since April, although they fell sharply in March.'

questions.prompt: Revenue ---- by fifteen percent so far this year.
questions.explanationTR: 'So far this year' describes an unfinished period connected to now, which needs the present perfect 'has grown'; the simple past 'grew' would require a finished time reference instead.

questions.prompt: The company ---- its earnings report last Tuesday.
questions.explanationTR: 'Last Tuesday' is a finished, dated time reference, so the past simple 'published' is required; the present perfect 'has published' is not used with a specific finished time like this.

questions.prompt: We ---- the new budget yet; the decision comes tomorrow.
questions.explanationTR: 'Yet' signals the present perfect in negative sentences about something that has not happened up to now ('haven't approved'); 'hadn't approved' refers to a time before another past event, and 'not approved' is missing its auxiliary verb.

questions.prompt: Profits ---- sharply in 2022, before recovering the following year.
questions.explanationTR: 'In 2022' is a specific, finished time reference, so the past simple 'fell' is correct; the present perfect 'have fallen' is not used with a dated past time like this.

questions.prompt: So far this quarter, the company ---- three new contracts.
questions.explanationTR: 'So far this quarter' describes a period that is still ongoing, so the present perfect 'has signed' is needed; 'signed' would wrongly treat the quarter as already finished.

questions.prompt: Turnover ---- significantly since the new product launched, according to the latest figures.
questions.explanationTR: 'Since' connects a past starting point to the present, which is a classic present perfect trigger ('has increased'); the simple past 'increased' does not fit with 'since' in this way.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that correctly reports a finished, dated result.
options: The board has approved the budget last month.
The board approved the budget last month.
The board have approved the budget last month.
The board was approving the budget last month.
The board approves the budget last month.
questions.explanationTR: 'Last month' is a finished, dated time reference, so the past simple 'approved' is correct; the present perfect forms 'has/have approved' cannot be combined with a specific finished time like 'last month', 'was approving' describes an activity in progress rather than a result, and 'approves' is present tense.

questions.prompt: Costs ---- steadily over the past six months, and they are still rising.
questions.explanationTR: 'Over the past six months' plus 'are still rising' shows an unfinished period connected to now, which needs the present perfect 'have risen'; the simple past 'rose' would suggest the rise is already over.

items.definition: A short quarterly report from a bicycle company and seven questions about its results

questions.prompt: What was Solara Bikes' revenue in the second quarter?
questions.explanationTR: The passage states that revenue reached eighteen million dollars; eleven million was the figure for expenses and sixty million was total assets, so those are tempting but incorrect distractors.

questions.prompt: Why did net income fall despite higher revenue?
options: The company paid a larger dividend to shareholders
Overhead costs rose and damaged inventory had to be written off
Revenue actually decreased during the quarter
The company sold several valuable assets
An audit found accounting errors from the previous year
questions.explanationTR: The passage directly explains that overhead costs increased faster than expected and that damaged inventory was written off; revenue did not fall, no larger dividend was mentioned, and the audit is only scheduled, not completed.

questions.prompt: What happened to shareholder equity during the quarter?
options: It stayed exactly the same as liabilities grew
It fell because liabilities increased faster than assets
It improved because assets grew while liabilities held steady
It disappeared due to the audit findings
It was paid out entirely as dividends
questions.explanationTR: The passage says total assets grew while liabilities stayed roughly the same, so shareholder equity improved; the other options reverse or invent details not in the text.

questions.prompt: How did the company improve its cash flow this quarter?
options: By raising the dividend for shareholders
By reducing the price of its electric bicycles
By collecting outstanding invoices more quickly
By writing off more inventory than planned
questions.explanationTR: The passage states that the finance team collected outstanding invoices more quickly, which helped cash flow; the other options are either not mentioned or describe unrelated events in the report.

questions.prompt: According to the report, what does management expect for the new factory?
options: It will close within a year due to losses
It will double its overhead costs
It will be sold before the next fiscal year
It will replace the electric bicycle line
It will break even within a year
questions.explanationTR: The passage says management expects the new factory to break even within a year; the other options describe outcomes the report never mentions.

questions.prompt: What is scheduled to happen next month?
options: An external audit will confirm the figures
The company will raise its dividend
A new forecast will replace this report
Shareholders will vote on new liabilities
questions.explanationTR: The passage ends by saying an external audit is scheduled for next month to confirm the figures; the other events are not mentioned as happening next month.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best summarizes the overall message of the report?
options: The company suffered a large loss and may have to close the new factory
Sales grew well, but net income dipped slightly and overhead needs attention
Revenue and net income both fell sharply this quarter
The company met every one of its financial targets with no concerns
Shareholders lost most of their equity due to a failed audit
questions.explanationTR: The closing paragraph says the quarter showed healthy growth in sales but a small decline in net income, and that overhead needs to be controlled; the other summaries contradict details stated earlier in the passage.

passage.title: Quarterly Report: Solara Bikes, Q2
passage.body:
Solara Bikes has published its results for the second quarter of the fiscal year. Revenue reached eighteen million dollars, an increase of nine percent year-on-year. Much of this growth came from strong demand in the electric bicycle line, which now makes up almost half of total turnover.

Despite the rise in revenue, net income fell slightly compared to the same quarter last year. Overhead costs, especially shipping and warehouse rent, increased faster than expected, and the company had to write off a batch of damaged inventory. Expenses for the quarter reached eleven million dollars, leaving a smaller profit margin than shareholders had hoped for.

The balance sheet remains healthy. Total assets grew to sixty million dollars, while liabilities stayed roughly the same, so shareholder equity improved. Cash flow was also positive: the finance team collected outstanding invoices more quickly, which helped the company avoid a cash shortage during a slow month.

Looking ahead, management issued a cautious forecast for the third quarter. They expect the new factory to break even within a year, and they do not plan to raise the dividend until earnings recover fully. An external audit is scheduled for next month to confirm the figures in this report before they are shared with investors.

Overall, the quarter showed healthy growth in sales but a small decline in net income. The board believes the company is still on track to meet its full-year targets, as long as overhead costs are brought under control before the next fiscal year begins.
